cornea.label: cornea
cornea.tip: The clear front window. It bends light even more than the lens does.

iris.label: iris
iris.tip: The colored ring. Its muscles make the pupil bigger or smaller.

pupil.label: pupil
pupil.tip: The hole in the iris that lets light in.

lens.label: lens
lens.tip: A clear, bendy disc that fine-tunes the focus for near or far things.

focusMuscle.label: ciliary muscle
focusMuscle.tip: The focus muscle: a ring that changes the lens's shape to focus near or far.

sclera.label: sclera
sclera.tip: The white of the eye: a tough outer wall that keeps the eye in shape.

choroid.label: choroid
choroid.tip: A dark layer full of blood vessels that feeds the retina.

vitreous.label: vitreous humor
vitreous.tip: Clear jelly that fills most of the eye and keeps it round. Light passes straight through it.

retina.label: retina
retina.tip: The light-sensing layer at the back, like the sensor in a camera.

blindSpot.label: optic disc
blindSpot.tip: Where the optic nerve leaves the eye. It has no light sensors, so it makes a blind spot. The brain fills it in with what's around it, so it goes unnoticed.

fovea.label: fovea
fovea.tip: The sharpest spot: a tiny pit packed with light sensors that sees the finest detail.

fovea2.label: temporal fovea
fovea2.tip: A second sharp spot, toward the temple.

opticNerve.label: optic nerve
opticNerve.tip: The cable that carries the picture to the brain.

wiring.label: nerve fiber layer
wiring.tip: The nerve wiring: fibers that collect the signals from the light sensors.

tapetum.label: tapetum lucidum
tapetum.tip: The night reflector: a shiny layer that bounces light back through the retina for a second chance. It makes eyes glow in the dark.

facet.label: corneal lens
facet.tip: A facet: one of the eye's tiny lenses, the top of one ommatidium (one little eye of many). Each facet sees just one dot of the picture; all the dots together make the image.

lightGuide.label: crystalline cone
lightGuide.tip: The light guide: a clear cone under each facet that funnels its light down to the sensors.

facetSensors.label: rhabdom
facetSensors.tip: The light sensors: a thin bundle of them under each facet. It adds up all the light from its facet into one dot, so more facets mean more dots.

pigment.label: pigment cells
pigment.tip: Dark cells packed between the tubes, so light from one facet can't leak into its neighbors.

superFacet.label: corneal lens
superFacet.tip: One of the eye's tiny lenses. Hundreds of them together focus light from one direction onto each sensor.

superCone.label: crystalline cone
superCone.tip: A clear cone that bends its light across the clear zone, to meet light from other facets on one sensor.

clearZone.label: clear zone
clearZone.tip: A clear gap between the lenses and the sensors, where light from many facets crosses over.

superSensors.label: rhabdom
superSensors.tip: The light sensors. Each collects light from hundreds of facets, so this eye works in very dim light.

superPigment.label: pigment cells
superPigment.tip: Dark pigment around the cones. In bright light it spreads down into the clear zone and blocks it, like a pupil closing.

eyeFloor.label: basement membrane
eyeFloor.tip: The floor of the eye, where the sensors' nerves leave for the brain.

nerveFibers.label: optic nerve fibers
nerveFibers.tip: Nerves from every facet's sensors, carrying the dots to the brain.

mirrorCornea.label: cornea
mirrorCornea.tip: The clear skin over the front of the eye.

mirrorIris.label: pupil rim
mirrorIris.tip: Dark pigment around the opening that lets light in.

mirrorLens.label: lens
mirrorLens.tip: A weak lens. The mirror does most of the focusing; the lens mainly sharpens its blur.

distalRetina.label: distal retina
distalRetina.tip: The front retina, near where the mirror focuses its light: it sees the sharper picture.

proximalRetina.label: proximal retina
proximalRetina.tip: The back retina. The light reaching it is out of focus, so it sees a blurrier picture.

eyeMirror.label: mirror
eyeMirror.tip: A curved mirror of tiny square crystals. It bounces light back forward, focused onto the retina.

eyeWall.label: pigment layer
eyeWall.tip: Dark pigment wrapping the eye, so light only gets in through the pupil.

scallopNerve.label: optic nerve
scallopNerve.tip: Carries signals from both retinas to the scallop's main nerve center.

uvLight.label: UV
uvLight.tip: Ultraviolet light, just past violet. A slightly yellow lens stops it before it reaches the retina; without that filter, the eye can see it. Faint rays: nothing here sees it.

irLight.label: IR
irLight.tip: Near-infrared light, just past red. It passes through the eye to the retina; only a sensor tuned far enough red can catch it. Faint rays: nothing here sees it.

settings.label: Number of facets
settings.tip: How many tiny eyes make up the dome. Each one sees one dot, so more facets give a finer picture. The angle between neighbors sets the size of the dots.

settings.label: Eye size
settings.tip: How wide the dome is. With the same number of facets, a bigger dome has bigger facets, and a bigger lens blurs less: light spreads out when it passes through a tiny opening.

settings.label: Eye design
settings.tip: How light gets from the facets to the sensors.

options.label: Apposition
options.tip: Each facet feeds only its own sensors. Sharp in daylight, poor at night. Most day insects.

options.label: Superposition
options.tip: Hundreds of facets focus onto each sensor across a clear zone: far brighter at night. Most moths and night beetles.

settings.label: Eye size
settings.tip: Bigger eyes see finer detail. Simplified: how much light reaches each point of the image depends on how wide the pupil is. Only a bigger eye can hold a much bigger pupil.

settings.label: Eye shape
settings.tip: Owls have tube-shaped eyes so huge eyes fit in a small skull.

options.label: Round
options.tip: A ball, like most eyes. It can turn in its socket.

options.label: Tube
options.tip: A wide back with a tube in front: room for a bigger lens and pupil, but a narrower view, and it can't turn in its socket.

settings.label: Retina type
settings.tip: Which way the light sensors (photoreceptors) point.

options.label: Inverted
options.tip: Sensors face away from the light, like in all vertebrates. The wiring sits in front of them and leaves through a hole: a blind spot.

options.label: Everted
options.tip: Sensors face toward the light, like in octopus and squid. The wiring sits behind them, so there is no blind spot.

settings.label: Focus
settings.tip: The distance the eye is focused on. Things nearer or farther look blurry.

settings.label: Pupil shape
settings.tip: The shape of the opening that lets light in.

options.label: Circular
options.tip: Round: the same in every direction.

options.label: Vertical slit
options.tip: Closes very tightly in bright light. Common in ambush hunters that are active day and night, like cats.

options.label: Horizontal slit
options.tip: A wide, flat opening that sees a broad strip of the ground or sea, like in goats and octopus.

settings.label: Pupil diameter
settings.tip: Pupil size in daylight; it opens wider in the dark. Wider is brighter but keeps less in focus; very narrow blurs by diffraction.

settings.label: Tapetum lucidum
settings.tip: Night reflector: a shiny layer that bounces light back through the retina. Brighter at night, but more glare.

options.label: Absent
options.tip: No reflector.

options.label: Present
options.tip: Light gets a second pass, and the eyes glow in the dark (eyeshine).

settings.label: Rods and cones
settings.tip: Rods work in dim light but can't see color. Cones see color and fine detail but need bright light. The example values are approximate.

settings.label: Sphere
settings.tip: Nearsighted or farsighted, in diopters, as on a glasses prescription. Myopia (nearsighted): the eyeball is a little too long, so far things blur. Emmetropia: normal. Hyperopia (farsighted): it is a little too short, so near things blur (try moving Focus, under the scene, toward Near).

settings.label: Astigmatism
settings.tip: The cornea is shaped a bit like a rugby ball instead of round, so blur stretches in one direction.

options.label: Absent
options.tip: A round cornea.

options.label: Present
options.tip: An oval cornea: things blur more in one direction.

settings.label: Cylinder
settings.tip: How oval the cornea is, in diopters: how much harder it focuses one way than the other. Written as a minus number on a glasses prescription.

settings.label: Axis
settings.tip: Which way the oval lies, in degrees, as on a prescription: 180 is horizontal, 90 vertical. Blur stretches at a right angle to it.

settings.label: Amblyopia
settings.tip: Lazy eye: the eye itself is healthy, but the brain learned to rely on it less. Focus and glasses can't fix it.

options.label: Absent
options.tip: The brain uses this eye fully.

options.label: Present
options.tip: The brain gives this eye's signal less weight: less sharp, less contrast.

settings.label: Severity
settings.tip: How strong it is: how much less the brain relies on this eye.

settings.label: Color vision
settings.tip: How many kinds of color sensors the eye has. More kinds tell more colors apart.

options.label: Monochromacy
options.tip: One kind of color sensor: shades of one color only.

options.label: Dichromacy
options.tip: Two kinds of color sensor: like most dogs and cats.

options.label: Trichromacy
options.tip: Three kinds of color sensor: like most people.

options.label: Tetrachromacy
options.tip: Four kinds of color sensor: like many birds, including ultraviolet.

options.label: Pentachromacy
options.tip: Five kinds of color sensor: more than any screen can show.

settings.label: Red-green deficiency
settings.tip: Red-green colorblindness: some people's red and green sensors are too alike, so reds and greens get confused.

options.label: Normal
options.tip: Reds and greens look different.

options.label: Deuteranomaly
options.tip: Red-green colorblind: the green sensor is shifted toward red, so reds and greens look more alike. The most common kind.

settings.label: Severity
settings.tip: From slightly mixed-up reds and greens to not telling them apart at all (at full strength this is called deuteranopia).

types.label: Cup eye
types.hint: A shallow pit lined with light sensors. No lens, no image: it only tells light from dark and roughly which direction light comes from.

types.label: Pinhole eye
types.hint: A deep cup with a tiny opening and no lens. Makes a dim, blurry image.

types.label: Camera eye
types.hint: One lens focuses light onto the back of the eye.

types.label: Compound eye
types.hint: A dome of many tiny eyes, each seeing one dot of the picture.

types.label: Mirror eye
types.hint: A curved mirror at the back bounces light forward onto the seeing layer.

examples.label: Cat

tapetum.label: tapetum cellulosum
tapetum.tip: The night reflector. A cat's is made of layers of reflecting cells. It bounces light back through the retina for a second chance, and makes the eyes glow in the dark.

fovea.label: area centralis
fovea.tip: The sharpest spot: a patch packed with cones, without the deep pit of a fovea.

examples.lensTip: Cats have no UV-sensing cone, so their colors start at violet. Their lenses still let some UV through (Douglas & Jeffery 2014), which only the rods may pick up, at night.

fovea.label: central fovea
fovea.tip: The deep fovea, the sharpest spot. It looks out to the side, about 45° from the beak.

fovea2.tip: A second, shallower fovea toward the temple. It looks forward, about 15° from the beak, where both eyes overlap.

cornea.tip: The clear front window. Underwater it barely bends light, since water bends light about as much as the eye itself does: the round lens does almost all the focusing.

fovea.label: visual streak
fovea.tip: Octopuses have no fovea. Their sharpest vision is a horizontal stripe across the retina, packed with light sensors.

lens.tip: A hard, round lens. It doesn't change shape: it slides toward the retina to focus far away, and forward for near things.

focusMuscle.label: lens muscle
focusMuscle.tip: A ring of muscle around the eye that moves the lens back and forth to focus.

examples.label: Whale

tips.pupilMm: From the bottlenose dolphin (Dawson et al. 1979). A humpback's is U-shaped in bright light.

examples.lensTip: The whale's lens cutoff is uncertain.

fovea.label: temporal area
fovea.tip: Whales have no fovea. Their sharpest vision is in two patches with more nerve cells; this one, toward the temple, is the larger and denser one.

fovea2.label: nasal area
fovea2.tip: The second, smaller patch with more nerve cells, toward the nose.

tapetum.label: tapetum fibrosum
tapetum.tip: The night reflector. A whale's is made of tightly packed collagen fibers, like a horse's or a cow's, not of cells like a cat's. It bounces light back through the retina for a second chance.

cornea.tip: The clear front window. Underwater it barely bends light, since water bends light about as much as the eye itself does: the round lens does almost all the focusing.

examples.label: Owl
examples.tip: A tawny owl. Owl color vision is debated: owls carry the genes for three kinds of cone, but how well they tell colors apart is unclear.
examples.lensTip: Owls have no UV-sensing cone (Höglund et al. 2019), so their colors start at violet. Their eyes still let some UV through, which only the rods may pick up, at night.

examples.label: Owl monkey
examples.tip: The only monkey active at night. It has no night reflector, so it relies on huge eyes instead.

fovea.label: rudimentary fovea
fovea.tip: A shallow, half-formed fovea, missing in many owl monkeys: with so few cones, the pit never fully forms.

examples.label: Fly
examples.tip: A house fly: about 3,500 facets in each eye.

examples.label: Bee
examples.tip: A honeybee worker: about 5,500 facets in each eye. It sees ultraviolet, blue and green, but not red.

examples.label: Moth
examples.tip: An elephant hawkmoth: a night flier that sees color even by starlight.

tips.facets: Set so facets sit 1.3° apart (Theobald et al. 2010). The total count isn't published.
tips.colors: Sensors at 350, 450 and 525 nm (Höglund et al. 1973).

examples.label: Scallop
examples.tip: A bay scallop. It has up to about 200 eyes, each under a millimeter, along the edge of its shell.
